items.name: Apple App Store Review Guidelines 2.3 Accurate Metadata and 5.2 Intellectual Property: what app names, subtitles, keywords, descriptions, screenshots and What's New text may contain
items.one_line: Apple's review rules for App Store listing copy: metadata must reflect the app's core experience, the app name is limited to 30 characters, no prices, trademarks, other apps or unverifiable claims in names and subtitles, 'For Kids' is reserved for the Kids Category, and What's New must describe significant changes.

items.name: Ayush (Ayurvedic, Siddha, Unani) drug advertisements: Drugs Rules rule 170, its 2024 omission and the Supreme Court orders of 2024-2025
items.one_line: Rule 170 required State approval (a Unique Identification Number) before any Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drug ad and barred disease-cure claims; the Ministry of Ayush omitted it on 1 Jul 2024, the Supreme Court stayed that on 27 Aug 2024 and vacated the stay on 11 Aug 2025, so as read in Oct 2026 the rule stands omitted while the DMR Act, D&C Act misbranding and ASCI / CCPA rules still bite.

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: OMITTED. The Supreme Court's order of 11 Aug 2025 records that the Ministry of Ayush notification of 01.07.2024 under the Drugs (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 2024 'had omitted Rule 170'; on 27.08.2024 the Court had ordered that 'Rule 170 shall remain on the statute book and in force' till further orders; on 11 Aug 2025 it disposed of the petition, reserved liberty to parties with 'any grievance with regard to the omission of Rule 170' and said 'interim order dated 27.08.2024 stands vacated'. A later challenge in another forum is possible: check before telling a client the rule is gone for good. The order PDF was read in a copy hosted by LiveLaw (the court's own site refused connections today); the Ministry of Ayush gazette notification itself was not read. Rules for a copywriter: (1) The former Rule 170 (as extracted in the order) barred ASU drug ads 'for the use of diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment or prevention of any disease, disorder, syndrome or condition', and made other ads wait for a Unique Identification Number from the State Licensing Authority; with the omission, no State pre-approval number is needed, but the cure-claim limits below still apply. (2) The Drugs and Magic Remedies Act, 1954 still bars ads suggesting a drug for its scheduled diseases in any medium (comp:dmr_act_1954). (3) Act s.33E(c): an Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drug is misbranded if anything accompanying it 'makes any false claim for the drug or which is false or misleading in any particular'. (4) The former Rule 170's rejection list is still a sound red-flag checklist (it mirrors DMR Act and ASCI risks): vulgarity or obscenity, sexual-organ or sexual-performance enhancement claims, 'photographs or testimonials of celebrities or government officials', references to a government body, a false impression of the drug's true character, and 'a misleading or exaggerated claim about the effectiveness'. (5) The ASCI Code and the CCPA 2022 guidelines apply to every ad regardless (comp:asci_code, comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022).

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: in force. Proposition 24 (November 2020) amended the CCPA and created the California Privacy Protection Agency, now styled ‘CalPrivacy’ (cppa.ca.gov). The regulations text is marked ‘Effective 1/1/2026’. RECENT CHANGE: the 2025 package (CCPA updates, risk assessments, cybersecurity audits, automated decisionmaking technology (ADMT), insurance) was adopted on July 24, 2025 and ‘approved by the Office of Administrative Law’ on September 22, 2025, effective January 1, 2026 (ccpa_updates page); a business already using ADMT for a significant decision must comply with the ADMT article ‘no later than January 1, 2027’ (regulations Article 11). A ‘Notices & Disclosures’ pre-rulemaking topic closed for comment on May 20, 2026 and is not yet a proposal. Rules for a writer: (1) Every disclosure must be ‘easy to read and understandable’ and ‘use plain, straightforward language and avoid technical or legal jargon’ (reg 7003(a)); readable on small screens, in the languages the business normally uses with Californians, and reasonably accessible to people with disabilities, following standards such as WCAG 2.1 for online notices (7003(b)). (2) Notice at Collection, at or before the point of collection: the categories of personal information (incl. sensitive), purposes, whether each category is sold or shared, how long each is kept or the criteria, the opt-out link and a privacy-policy link (7012(e)); a link must land on the exact section, not the top of the policy (7012(f)); ‘the business shall not collect’ without it (7012(d)). (3) Privacy policy: online and offline practices, categories collected in the preceding 12 months, sources, purposes, what is sold or shared and to whom, every CCPA right, how to exercise it, and the ‘Date the privacy policy was last updated’ (7011(e)), behind a conspicuous link using the word ‘privacy’ (7011(d)); the statute requires updating ‘at least once every 12 months’ (Civil Code 1798.130(a)(5)). (4) Exact link titles: “Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information” and “Limit the Use of My Sensitive Personal Information” (Civil Code 1798.135(a)), in the homepage header or footer (7013(c), 7014(c)); or one link titled ‘Your Privacy Choices’ or ‘Your California Privacy Choices’ with the opt-out icon beside it (7015(b)); links at least the size and colour of neighbouring links (7003(c)). (5) Choice wording must be symmetrical: ‘Accept All’ with ‘Decline All’, not only ‘More Information’; ‘Yes’ with ‘No’, not ‘Ask me later’; no double negatives such as Yes/No beside a do-not-sell statement; no false-urgency countdowns (7004(a)); consent obtained by a dark pattern ‘shall not constitute consumer consent’ (7004(b)). (6) ADMT Pre-use Notice: a ‘plain language explanation of the specific purpose’, never just ‘to make a significant decision’ (7220(c)(1)); the site must display whether an opt-out preference signal was honoured, e.g. ‘Opt-Out Request Honored’ (7025(c)(6)). Penalty: fines adjusted for 2025 to not more than USD 2,663 per violation or USD 7,988 per intentional violation or violation involving known under-16s (cpi_adjustment page). Other US state privacy laws: not read in this pass. Related: comp:gdpr_marketing_consent, comp:coppa, comp:wcag_22, comp:ccpa_dark_patterns_2023 (India's CCPA, a different body).

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: the 2020 Rules are in force since publication on 23 July 2020; the only 2021 amendment notified (G.S.R. 328(E), 17 May 2021) changed rule 4(1) on incorporation only; the June-July 2021 draft amendments (flash sales, mis-selling, cross-selling) were a consultation draft and are not listed among the notified instruments on the Department's page; the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) (Amendment) Rules, 2026 are dated 9 September 2026 and come into force from 1st January (the year digits did not extract from the official PDF; secondary reports say 1 January 2027). Until then the 2020 text applies. Rules for a copywriter writing listings, seller pages and sale banners: (1) Seller listings must show 'total price in single figure' with the break-up of compulsory and voluntary charges (delivery, handling, tax), the expiry date where applicable, country of origin, importer details for imports, grievance officer, and accurate exchange, return, refund (incl. 'costs of return shipping'), delivery and warranty information (rule 6(5)); the 2026 amendment adds best-before or use-before date and any GSTIN or MSME registration number. (2) Fake reviews: no seller or inventory entity shall 'falsely represent itself as a consumer and post reviews' or misrepresent the quality or features of goods (rules 6(2), 7(2)); ads must be 'consistent with the actual characteristics, access and usage conditions' (rules 6(4)(c), 7(3)). (3) No price manipulation to impose an 'unjustified price' (rule 4(11)(a)); no consent recorded automatically, 'including in the form of pre-ticked checkboxes' (rule 4(9)); no cancellation charge unless the entity bears similar charges (rule 4(8)). (4) From the 2026 amendment: a price reduction must show the 'prior price', defined as 'the lowest price of a good or service thirty days prior to the announcement of price reduction'; sponsored listings must be 'distinctly identified with clear and prominent disclosures'; no misleading users 'by manipulating search result or search indexes'; marketplaces show seller name, address, customer care, ratings and the main ranking parameters in plain language; country of origin by its full name as under the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules; the seller's name on the invoice in the same font size as the platform's; a yearly dark-pattern self-audit with a displayed certificate. items.note: In force. Read 2026-10-13 on the Health Ministry's NTCP site: the Act (Act 34 of 2003; scanned gazette copy, so wording below is copied with care from imperfect OCR), the 2005 amendment rules (G.S.R. 345(E)), the film and TV rules in force from 2 Oct 2012 (G.S.R. 708(E)) and the OTT rule notified 31 May 2023 (G.S.R. 400(E), in force three months after publication). The 2011 amendments (G.S.R. 619(E) and 786(E)) are image-only scans and were not read, so later changes to rule 4 may exist. India Code timed out today. Rules for a copywriter: (1) s.5(1): no tobacco producer or distributor may advertise, no one controlling a medium may carry a tobacco ad, and no person shall 'take part in any advertisement which directly or indirectly suggests or promotes the use or consumption' of tobacco, so the agency, writer and creator are covered. (2) 'Advertisement' includes any visible representation by notice, circular, label or wrapper and any announcement made orally or by light, sound, smoke or gas (s.3(a)). (3) s.5(3): no promotion of tobacco or of 'any trade mark or brand name' of tobacco in exchange for a sponsorship, gift, prize or scholarship. (4) Indirect advertisement (rule 2(e), 2005) covers: using a tobacco name or brand to market other goods, services and events; marketing tobacco under a brand known for other goods; using colours, layout or presentation associated with a tobacco product; and using tobacco products and smoking situations when advertising other goods and services. (5) The only advertising exceptions are on the pack itself and at the entrance or inside a shop selling tobacco (s.5(2) proviso); the 2005 rule 4 limits such a board to 60 cm by 45 cm with a warning 'Tobacco causes cancer' or 'Tobacco kills', and no brand pack shot, brand name or promotional message. (6) New films and TV programmes showing tobacco (rule 8, 2012) need an editorial justification to the CBFC, anti-tobacco health spots of at least thirty seconds at the beginning and middle, a static warning at the bottom of the screen while tobacco is shown, and an audio-visual disclaimer of at least twenty seconds at the beginning and middle, in the language of the film (or of its dub or subtitles); warnings are 'Smoking causes cancer' or 'Smoking kills' for smoking and 'Tobacco causes cancer' or 'Tobacco kills' for smokeless tobacco, black on white. (7) OTT (rule 11, 2023): a publisher of online curated content (which includes films, series, documentaries 'podcasts and other such content') showing tobacco must run the same spots, static warning and 20-second disclaimer in the content's language, and may not show 'the brands of cigarettes or other tobacco products or any form of tobacco product placement', or tobacco in promotional materials such as trailers. items.note: In force. Read 2026-10-13 in CDSCO's own PDFs: the Drugs Rules in CDSCO's compiled version (amended to G.S.R. 360(E) of 1 Jul 2024; CDSCO says it is a compilation, not the gazette), the Cosmetics Rules, 2020 as notified (later amendments not checked), and the Act in CDSCO's compilation to 31 Dec 2016. Penalties were not read, so none are stated. Rules for a copywriter: (1) Drugs Rules rule 106(1): no drug may claim to prevent or cure a Schedule J disease, nor 'convey to the intending user thereof any idea that it may prevent or cure' one. 'Convey any idea' catches implied claims, before-and-after visuals and testimonials, not only the words 'cures'. (2) Schedule J (51 entries) includes AIDS, cancer, diabetes, high/low blood pressure, obesity, baldness, change in colour of the hair and growth of new hair, premature greying of hair, fairness of the skin, premature ageing, power to rejuvenate, improvement in height of children/adults, increase in brain capacity and improvement of memory, improvement in vision, jaundice/hepatitis/liver disorders, piles and fistulae, kidney and gall-bladder stones, sexual impotence and sexual-performance claims, and form or structure of breast. (3) Rule 106(2): no drug may claim to procure or assist to procure miscarriage. (4) Act s.17(c) (and s.33E(c) for Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drugs): a drug is misbranded if its label, container 'or anything accompanying the drug' makes 'any false claim for the drug' or is 'false or misleading in any particular'. (5) Cosmetics Rules rule 36: 'No cosmetic may purport or claim to purport or convey any idea which is false or misleading to the intending user'; Act s.17C(c) makes a cosmetic misbranded for a false or misleading statement on the label or 'anything accompanying' it. (6) A cosmetic is defined by use for 'cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness, or altering the appearance' (Act s.3(aaa)); CDSCO FAQ Q.54: 'Products having drug claim do not come under the definition of cosmetic', so 'treats acne', 'cures dandruff' or 'heals' copy on a cosmetic is a drug claim. (7) Labels must carry the rule 34 particulars (name, manufacturer and address or 'Made in', expiry or use-before, batch number, manufacturing licence number, net contents, safety directions where a hazard exists); hair dyes need the rule 37 caution legend in English and local languages. items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: Article 6a of Directive 98/6/EC was inserted by Directive (EU) 2019/2161, applied from 28 May 2022 (2019/2161), and is shown in the consolidated text of 28.05.2022. Text: ‘Any announcement of a price reduction shall indicate the prior price applied by the trader’ (Art 6a(1)); the prior price is the ‘lowest price applied by the trader during a period of time not shorter than 30 days prior to the application of the price reduction’ (Art 6a(2)). Exceptions are Member State options, so check the national law: different rules for ‘goods which are liable to deteriorate or expire rapidly’ (6a(3)); a shorter period where the product has been on the market for less than 30 days (6a(4)); for a progressively increased reduction, the prior price may be the price before the first reduction (6a(5)). CJEU, Case C-330/23 (a consumer association against a supermarket chain), judgment of 26 September 2024: a reduction announced ‘in the form of a percentage, or in the form of a promotional statement intended to highlight the advantageous nature of the announced price’ must be determined on the basis of the prior price. Commission guidance 2021: (1) covers ‘20 % off’, crossed-out ‘was’ prices, and announcements like ‘sales’ price, ‘special offers’ or ‘Black Friday offers’; the lowest price must include any earlier promotional price in the 30 days; worked example: ‘50 % off’ with a 30-day low of EUR 100 must show EUR 100 even though the last selling price was EUR 160. (2) Applies to goods only, not services or digital content (those stay under the UCPD), in shops and online. (3) Out of scope but still under the UCPD: ‘best/lowest prices’ claims, comparisons with recommended retail price or other sellers, tied offers like ‘buy one, get two’, genuine loyalty programmes and personalised vouchers; a discount code available to most customers is in scope. (4) A general banner (‘20 % off on everything today’) need not show the prior price on the banner, but each price tag or online price section must. (5) Extra reference prices are allowed only if clearly explained; ‘up to 70 % off’ when few items reach 70 % may breach the UCPD. Penalties are set nationally (Art 8 of the consolidated text). Related: comp:eu_ucpd.

RECENT CHANGE: Directive (EU) 2024/825 amends the UCPD again and Member States ‘shall apply those measures from 27 September 2026’ (2024/825); the consolidated text read does not yet include it. A directive works through each Member State's national law. Rules for a copywriter: (1) Misleading action: copy is misleading if it deceives ‘including overall presentation’, ‘even if the information is factually correct’, about e.g. the price, main characteristics or ‘the results to be expected from its use’ (Art 6(1), consolidated text). (2) Misleading omission: hiding material information or giving it ‘in an unclear, unintelligible, ambiguous or untimely manner’, or failing to identify commercial intent (Art 7(2)); an invitation to purchase must give the main characteristics, trader identity and address, and ‘the price inclusive of taxes’ plus delivery charges (Art 7(4)); where reviews are shown, how the trader checks they come from real buyers is material (Art 7(6)); search tools must explain the main ranking parameters (Art 7(4a)). (3) Annex I blacklist, unfair in all circumstances: bait advertising (point 5); ‘Falsely stating that a product will only be available for a very limited time’ (7); undisclosed paid editorial, advertorial (11); search results without ‘clearly disclosing any paid advertisement or payment specifically for achieving higher ranking’ (11a); falsely claiming a product cures illnesses (17); calling a product ‘gratis’, ‘free’, ‘without charge’ if the consumer pays anything beyond unavoidable response and delivery costs (20); falsely representing oneself as a consumer (22); claiming reviews come from real users ‘without taking reasonable and proportionate steps to check’ (23b); submitting or commissioning ‘false consumer reviews or endorsements’ or misrepresenting reviews (23c). (4) Commission guidance 2021: a ‘free’ offer may not charge for packaging, handling or administration (section 3.4); review misrepresentation includes ‘Publishing only positive reviews and deleting the negative ones’ and pre-filled positive review templates (4.2.4); influencer disclosure is inadequate as ‘hashtags at the end of a lengthy disclaimer; merely tagging a trader’ or behind ‘read more’, and free products or affiliate commission count as consideration (4.2.6). (5) From 27 Sep 2026 (2024/825 Annex): new blacklist points ban a generic environmental claim without ‘recognised excellent environmental performance relevant to the claim’ (4a), whole-product claims about one aspect (4b), offsetting-based ‘neutral, reduced or positive impact’ claims (4c) and sustainability labels not based on a certification scheme or public authority (2a). Penalty (Art 13 as amended): in coordinated cross-border enforcement the maximum fine must be ‘at least 4 % of the trader’s annual turnover in the Member State or Member States concerned’, or at least EUR 2 million where turnover data is unavailable. Related: comp:eu_prior_price_rule, comp:eu_dsa_ad_transparency, comp:uk_dmcc_schedule20, comp:ftc_consumer_reviews_rule, comp:bis_is_19000_online_reviews.

items.name: European Accessibility Act, Directive (EU) 2019/882: accessibility requirements for products and services, incl. e-commerce, e-books, consumer banking and passenger transport information
items.one_line: Since 28 June 2025 covered products and consumer services in the EU (e-commerce sites and apps, e-books, consumer banking, passenger-transport websites, apps and tickets, telecoms, AV-media access) must be accessible, and their information must be understandable, perceivable, available as usable text and backed by text alternatives; microenterprises providing services are exempt.

sources.title: EU Publications Office: Directive (EU) 2019/882 on the accessibility requirements for products and services, OJ L 151, 7.6.2019
sources.supports: Article 2 scope and exclusions, Article 3 definitions (microenterprise, e-commerce services), Article 4(5) microenterprise exemption, Article 13 and Annex V service information, Annex I Sections I, III and IV, Article 30 penalties, Articles 31-32 application and transitional dates

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: in application; Member States had to adopt national laws by 28 June 2022 and ‘shall apply those measures from 28 June 2025’ (Art 31). It covers products ‘placed on the market after 28 June 2025’ and services ‘provided to consumers after 28 June 2025’ (Art 2). Transitional: service contracts agreed before 28 June 2025 may continue ‘no longer than five years from that date’, and a transitional period ends on 28 June 2030 for products already used to provide services (Art 32). Scope (Art 2): products include computers and operating systems, payment terminals, ATMs, ticketing and check-in machines, consumer terminal equipment used for electronic communications or audiovisual media, and e-readers; services include electronic communications, access to audiovisual media, websites, apps, e-tickets and travel information of air, bus, rail and waterborne passenger transport, consumer banking, ‘e-books and dedicated software’ and ‘e-commerce services’. Not covered (Art 2(4)): pre-recorded time-based media and office files published before 28 June 2025, third-party content not funded, developed or controlled by the operator, and archive content not updated after that date. Rules for a writer: (1) Service information must be made available ‘via more than one sensory channel’, ‘presented in an understandable way’, in text formats usable for assistive formats, and ‘supplementing any non-textual content with an alternative presentation’ (Annex I Section III(b)): every image, icon or video in product, help or checkout copy needs a text alternative or captions. (2) Websites and apps must be accessible by making them ‘perceivable, operable, understandable and robust’ (Section III(c)), the same four principles WCAG uses (see comp:wcag_22). (3) Consumer banking information must be understandable ‘without exceeding a level of complexity superior to level B2 (upper intermediate)’ of the CEFR (Section IV(e)). (4) E-commerce must provide ‘the information concerning accessibility of the products and services being sold’ when the responsible operator supplies it (Section IV(g)); e-books must be discoverable ‘by providing information through metadata about their accessibility features’ (Section IV(f)). (5) Service providers must explain how the service meets the requirements in ‘the general terms and conditions, or equivalent document’ (Annex V), available in written and oral format and accessibly (Art 13(2)): someone has to write an accessibility statement. (6) Product labelling, instructions and warnings must be understandable and in fonts of adequate size with sufficient contrast (Annex I Section I). Exemption: ‘Microenterprises providing services shall be exempt’ from the service accessibility requirements (Art 4(5)); a microenterprise ‘employs fewer than 10 persons’ with turnover or balance sheet not over EUR 2 million (Art 3). Penalties are set by each Member State and must be ‘effective, proportionate and dissuasive’ (Art 30). Related: comp:wcag_22, comp:rpwd_act_accessibility.

items.name: Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act, 1986
items.one_line: Criminal law: no one may publish, arrange or take part in any advertisement, or produce, sell or circulate any book, film, photograph, painting or figure, that depicts a woman's figure, form or body in a way that is indecent, derogatory to or denigrating women, or likely to deprave or corrupt public morality.

items.note: In force (central Act 60 of 1986). India Code refused the connection twice on 2026-10-13 (timeout, then HTTP 403), so the text was read in a Government of Tripura transcription, a secondary copy with small typing errors: confidence medium; check India Code before quoting a section in a legal document. Amendments after 1986 were not checked. Rules for a copywriter: (1) Definition (s.2): 'indecent representation of women' means depicting the figure of a woman, her form or body or any part of it so as to be 'indecent, or derogatory to, or denigrating women', or 'likely to deprave, corrupt or injure the public morality or morals'. (2) s.3: 'No person shall publish, or cause to be published, or arrange or take part in the publication or exhibition of' an advertisement containing it 'in any form': the brand, agency, copywriter, model, publisher and influencer are all within 'take part'. (3) 'Advertisement' includes any notice, circular, label, wrapper or other document and 'any visible representation made by means of any light, sound, smoke or gas', so packaging and labels count. (4) s.4 bans producing, selling, hiring out, distributing, circulating or posting any book, pamphlet, paper, slide, film, writing, drawing, painting, photograph, representation or figure containing it; exceptions are material justified as being for the public good in the interest of science, literature, art or learning, material kept or used bona fide for religious purposes, sculpture or paintings on ancient monuments or temples, and films governed by Part II of the Cinematograph Act, 1952 (certified films are handled by the CBFC instead). (5) Penalty as printed in this copy (s.6): first conviction up to two years' imprisonment and fine up to two thousand rupees; second or later conviction six months to five years and fine of ten thousand to one lakh rupees; offences are cognizable and bailable (s.8); company officers in charge are liable unless they prove due diligence (s.7). items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: Part III is in the MeitY consolidated text (updated as on 10.02.2026) and is administered by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. On 14 Aug 2021 the Bombay High Court, as interim relief, directed 'stay of operation of sub-rules (1) and (3) of Rule 9' (the duty to adhere to the Code of Ethics and the three-tier structure); on 22 Mar 2024 the Supreme Court transferred the High Court challenges to the Delhi High Court and disposed of the Union's appeals against that interim order by letting it seek relief there. A secondary report (Nov 2024) says the Delhi High Court split the hearing into Part II and Part III and listed it for 13 Jan 2025; this pass found no Delhi High Court ruling on Part III. So never tell a client the Code is enforceable against them through rule 9, and never tell them Part III is struck down: say it is under challenge with an interim stay of rule 9(1) and 9(3). Rules a writer must remember: (1) Who is covered: a 'publisher of news and current affairs content' means an online paper, news portal, news aggregator, news agency or similar, but not newspapers, replica e-papers, or an individual who is not publishing 'in the course of systematic business, professional or commercial activity' (rule 2(1)(t)). (2) News code (Appendix I): the PCI Norms of Journalistic Conduct, the Programme Code under section 5 of the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995, and no content prohibited by law. (3) OTT code (Appendix II): every title is rated U, U/A 7+, U/A 13+, U/A 16+ or A, with the rating and a content descriptor shown 'at the beginning of every programme', and publishers must strive to put the rating on promos; parental locks for U/A 13+ and above, age verification for A. (4) Grievances (rule 10): acknowledge within twenty-four hours, decide within fifteen days, appeal to the self-regulating body within fifteen days, then to the Ministry oversight mechanism within fifteen days; the self-regulating body can require an apology, a warning card or disclaimer, or reclassification (rule 12). (5) A Grievance Officer based in India with contact details shown on the site (rule 11), a monthly compliance report (rule 18), and records of content kept for at least sixty days (rule 19). AI and synthetic content duties of intermediaries are a separate item: comp:it_rules_sgi_2026.

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: self-regulation that binds only Members and Associate Members of the News Broadcasters & Digital Association, for their TV channels and digital news platforms; the Regulations PDF is dated 20.06.2024 with 'Amended: 03.12.2024'. The Code of Conduct is the Code of Ethics plus Guidelines and Advisories. Rules a writer must remember: (1) Accuracy before speed: 'Errors must be corrected promptly and clearly, whether in the use of pictures, a news report, a caption, a graphic or a script' (Code); allegations are reported accurately as made, agency copy is attributed, archive footage is labelled 'file' with the date of first broadcast, reconstructions are clearly marked, and facts are kept apart from opinion, analysis and comment (Reportage guidelines). (2) Crime and courts: do not glamorise or sensationalise crime or suicide, do not show techniques that may tempt imitation, do not prejudge a sub judice matter, no close-ups of dead or mutilated bodies, no identification of victims of sexual crimes against women and children (Reportage 3). (3) Privacy: no disclosure of where a person or family lives without permission; interviews of the injured, victims or grieving only with prior consent (Reportage 5). (4) Harmony: avoid racial and religious stereotyping (Reportage 9); anchors must not make 'derisive or derogatory statements about individuals, communities or religious beliefs' and must not project allegations as facts without verification from a credible source (Anchors guidelines, 2022). (5) Complaints: first to the broadcaster within 15 days of the broadcast, the broadcaster answers within 15 days, then to the NBDSA within 15 days (Guide). Penalties in the Regulations run from warning, admonition or censure to fines of up to Rs 2 lacs for a first violation, rising to 1% of turnover capped at Rs 25 lakhs, with removal or editing of the content on digital platforms and social media.

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: the current edition is 2022 (the Council Norms page lists it, plus further norms approved on 17.11.2023 and 28.03.2024 that this pass did not read). It is the Council's self-regulatory code under the Press Council Act, 1978 for print newspapers, news agencies and journalists; the IT Rules 2021 Appendix names the same Norms as the code for digital news publishers (that route is under an interim stay, see comp:it_rules_2021_digital_news_code). Any person may complain to the Council, after first writing to the editor (Part D). Rules a writer must remember: (1) Accuracy: the press shall eschew 'inaccurate, baseless, graceless, misleading or distorted material', report all sides of the core issue, and not set out rumours and surmises as facts; a report based on an FIR that is critical of someone must say it rests only on the FIR and also carry the affected party's version (norm 1). (2) Headlines: 'Headings must reflect and justify the matter printed under them', and a heading that carries an allegation names its source or uses quotation marks (norm 17). (3) Caste and community: an accused or victim 'shall not be described by his caste or community' when it has nothing to do with the offence (norm 4). (4) Corrections are published suo motu, promptly and with due prominence, with an apology for a serious lapse (norm 9); a person affected by a report gets the right of reply, published promptly, with due prominence and free of cost (norm 41). (5) Suicide: no prominent or repeated stories, no method, no site details, no sensational headlines, no photographs, video footage or social media links (norm 39(b)); crime and courts: an accused is presumed innocent and reports should not lead the public to believe in the person's complicity (norm 43(a)). (6) Advertorials similar to news carry the heading 'Advertisement/Advertorials' in bold, and supplements say 'Marketing Initiative' (norms 2 and 29). items.note: In force: the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 apply 'with effect from April 1, 2026' (text read as amended up to July 7, 2026); the Master Circular of March 20, 2026 replaced the one of June 27, 2024; AMFI's Master Circular for MFDs is dated January 14, 2026. All read 2026-10-13 on sebi.gov.in and amfiindia.com. Rules for a copywriter: (1) Scope: an advertisement is 'any communication issued by or on behalf of the mutual fund or asset management company that may influence the investment decision' (reg 2(c)), so social posts, reels, emails and creator scripts count. (2) Fifth Schedule: ads must be 'accurate, true, fair, clear, complete, unambiguous and concise'; no statements 'based on assumption/projections', no 'testimonials or any ranking based on any criteria', no exaggerated slogan inconsistent with the risk-return profile, 'No celebrities shall form part of the advertisement', no discrediting other ads or unfair comparisons. (3) Standard warning, word for word: 'Mutual Fund investments are subject to market risks, read all scheme related documents carefully.' No words added or removed; in the ad's own language for a vernacular ad; in audio-visual ads both shown and voiced, e.g. 'fourteen (14) words running for at least five (5) seconds'. (4) Performance ads (Master Circular ch. 14): CAGR for at least 1, 3 and 5 years and since inception, plus point-to-point returns on a Rs 10,000 investment, computed to the last month-end before the ad; say whether regular or direct plan; show the benchmark and the additional benchmark; add other schemes of the same fund manager; 'Where the scheme has been in existence for less than six months, past performance shall not be provided.' (5) A Specialized Investment Fund ad carries its own fixed warning (para 21.13.5), beginning 'Investments in Specialized Investment Fund involves relatively higher risk including potential loss of capital, liquidity risk and market volatility.' (6) Distributors (AMFI): show 'AMFI-registered Mutual Fund Distributor' with name and ARN (at least font size 12 in print, legible on websites, apps and all other communication); 'not provide any indicative portfolio or indicative yield or indicative return'; use AMC marketing material 'as is'; no 'Adviser', 'Wealth Manager' or 'Consultant' in the name unless SEBI-registered; on YouTube and social media, education only, no scheme-specific recommendations or performance claims, disclose MFD status and ARN; no 'free advise' or 'free portfolio review' lures (FAQ). Cross-reference comp:sebi_finfluencer_association and comp:asci_influencer.

items.note: In force; both master circulars dated February 06, 2026 (read 2026-10-13 on sebi.gov.in) carry the code first issued by circulars of April 05 and April 06, 2023 (IA footnote). Rules for a copywriter: (1) Scope: 'all forms of communications' by or on behalf of the IA or RA that may influence investment decisions, expressly including email, text messaging, messaging platforms, 'social media platforms', radio, TV and video. (2) Must show: name as registered with SEBI, registered office address, SEBI registration number, logo or brand name, CIN if any; on SMS, pop-ups and social media where these do not fit, a hyperlink to the official website that carries them. (3) Standard warning in at least 10-point font, word for word: 'Investment in securities market are subject to market risks. Read all the related documents carefully before investing'; in audio-visual ads shown and voiced, e.g. '20 words running for at least 10 seconds'; accurately translated in a non-English ad. Securities shown as examples need 'The securities quoted are for illustration only and are not recommendatory'. Ads and client communication carry the disclaimer that begins 'Registration granted by SEBI, enlistment with IAASB and certification from NISM' and ends 'in no way guarantee performance of the IA or provide any assurance of returns to investors' (the RA version names BSE and 'the intermediary'). (4) Banned: false, misleading, biased or deceptive statements 'based on assumptions or projections'; 'Any misleading or deceptive testimonials'; calling a report or service free unless it is free without condition; any promise of assured or risk-free return, and no implied 'minimum returns or target return or percentage accuracy'; discrediting other intermediaries; past performance or risk-return metrics unless verified by the Past Risk and Return Verification Agency (PaRRVA) and claimed as SEBI specifies; superlatives such as 'Best', 'No. 1', 'Top Adviser', 'Leading' (factual awards from independent organisations are allowed). (5) 'Advertisements shall not include SEBI Logo'; prior approval of the ad from the SEBI-recognised supervisory body; no games, leagues or competitions with prizes; a suspended IA or RA may not advertise; keep a copy of each ad for five years. Cross-reference comp:sebi_finfluencer_association (who a regulated entity may associate with) and comp:asci_influencer.

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: CCPA guideline 6 in force since the 2022 notification; the Cable TV rule read as on 02.01.2025; ASCI criteria dated November 23rd, 2023; the CCPA (06 Mar 2024) and MIB (21 Mar 2024) advisories on betting are in force as advisories; the Health Ministry's March 2025 letter to the IPL is a request, not a rule. Press reports of draft CCPA rules on celebrity surrogate endorsements (late 2024) were not traced to any notification in this pass: do not cite them as law. Rules for a copywriter: (1) A surrogate advertisement is one for goods whose advertising is prohibited or restricted, made 'by circumventing such prohibition or restriction and portraying it to be an advertisement for other goods' (CCPA 2(h), 6(1)). (2) It is surrogate if it 'indicates or suggests directly or indirectly' the banned product, or 'uses any brand name, logo, colour, layout and presentation associated with' it (6(2)); the proviso saves 'mere use of a brand name or company name' shared with the banned product only if the ad is not otherwise objectionable. (3) On TV and cable, a brand-extension ad must show only the product advertised, make no direct or indirect reference to the prohibited product, contain no 'nuances or phrases promoting prohibited products', use no associated colours, layout or presentation and no 'situations typical for promotion of prohibited products'; the advertiser also needs a Chartered Accountant's certificate of real distribution and proportionate spend, an MIB finding of genuine brand extension and CBFC certification before telecast (rule 7(2)(viii)). (4) ASCI test: the extension is registered with an authority (GST, FDA, FSSAI, TM); a brand over two years old needs turnover above Rs 5 crore a year nationally or Rs 1 crore per state; a newer one needs one of Rs 20 lakh a month in sales, Rs 10 crore of exclusive fixed assets, long-term supply contracts, or turnover above 10% of the restricted brand's; the ad budget may not exceed 200% of the extension's sales in years 1 and 2, 100% in year 3, 50% in year 4 and 30% after; failing means 'a surrogate created to advertise a restricted category'. (5) Tobacco has its own indirect-advertising definition (comp:cotpa_tobacco_advertising). (6) Betting: the CCPA says celebrities and influencers promoting online betting are 'equally liable for participating in an illegal activity', and the MIB told influencers to refrain from promoting offshore betting 'including surrogate advertisements', with removal of posts or accounts as a consequence; online money games are covered by comp:online_gaming_act_2025. items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: statutory code under section 123 of the DPA 2018, 'laid before Parliament on 11 June 2020 and issued on 12 August 2020'; it 'comes into force on 2 September 2020' with a 12-month transition (ICO, About this code). Change: the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 added a 'children's higher protection matters' duty to the UK GDPR data protection by design rules (ICO guidance updated 5 Feb 2026); the ICO says on 19 June 2026 that 'all data protection provisions in the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 are now in force'. The duty 'applies to the same online services that are in scope of our children's code' and 'if you already conform to the code, you are likely to comply with this duty'. No change to the code's own standards was shown on the code pages read. Rules for a copywriter: (1) Scope: 'information society services likely to be accessed by children' in the UK, including apps, games, social media, streaming, news, educational and retail sites; 'It is not restricted to services specifically directed at children.' (2) Standard 4: privacy information, terms, policies and community standards 'must be concise, prominent, and in clear language suited to the age of the child', plus 'bite-sized' explanations at the point a data use is activated (a just-in-time notice), with a prompt to speak to an adult where risk calls for it; information must not 'promise protections or standards that are not routinely upheld'; legal terms may carry child-friendly explanations alongside; use diagrams, cartoons, video, icons and layered text, tailored by age. (3) Standard 6: 'Uphold your own published terms, policies and community standards'. (4) Standard 7: 'Settings must be high privacy by default' unless there is a compelling reason; optional uses must be individually activated by the child, and copy must not nudge towards a lower privacy option. (5) Standard 13: 'Do not use nudge techniques to lead or encourage children to provide unnecessary personal data or turn off privacy protections'; no exploiting colours, imagery or affirmation needs, no pre-selected older age range; pro-privacy and wellbeing nudges (breaks, pause and save) are encouraged.

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: in force in stages. The criminal offences 'came into effect on 31 January 2024' (GOV.UK explainer; CPS says Part 10 'came into force from 31 January 2024'). Ofcom's dates page (updated 24 Aug 2026): Part 5 pornography publishers must use highly effective age assurance from January 2025 (government commenced the duty 17 Jan 2025); 'Illegal content Codes of Practice comes into force' 17 Mar 2025; 'Protection of Children Codes of Practice come into force' 25 Jul 2025; CSEA reporting duty 7 Apr 2026; register of categorised services due July 2026 (TBC). The Act text on legislation.gov.uk returned a bot challenge and was not read (not bypassed): rules below come from GOV.UK, Ofcom and CPS pages. Rules for a copywriter: (1) Scope: 'The Act's duties apply to search services and services that allow users to post content online', including providers outside the UK 'should they have links to the UK' (GOV.UK). (2) Terms of service: Ofcom wants terms 'clear and accessible'; under code measure ICU G3 the protection provisions must be 'clearly signposted for the general public', 'laid out and formatted in a way that helps United Kingdom users read and understand them', 'written to a reading age comprehensible for the youngest individual permitted to use the service without the consent of a parent or guardian', and usable with keyboard navigation and screen readers (Ofcom code). Under ICU G1 they must say how users are protected from illegal content, how reported content is swiftly taken down, any proactive technology used, and how complaints are handled. (3) Age limits: social media companies must 'enforce their age limits consistently' and state their age-assurance measures in the terms; Category 1 services must 'uphold their terms of service' (GOV.UK). (4) False communications offence: sending a message that 'conveys information that the person knows to be false', intending it to 'cause non-trivial psychological or physical harm', with no reasonable excuse (CPS). (5) Threatening communications offence: a message that 'conveys a threat of death or serious harm', sent intending or reckless as to whether the reader fears it will be carried out; serious harm includes grievous bodily harm, rape, assault by penetration or 'serious financial loss' (CPS). The exemption of recognised news publishers from the false communications offence was not confirmed on any page read.

items.note: Status as read 2026-10-13: policy page 'Last updated: September 23, 2026'; the AI Providers clause sits in the Meta Terms for WhatsApp Business Platform (section 4.7, 'Last Modified: September 23, 2026'); its 15 Jan 2026 start date comes only from news coverage (TechCrunch, secondary), not an official page. Template field limits live in plat:whatsapp_business_template: cross-reference, do not repeat. Rules for a copywriter: (1) Opt-in: message people only if they gave you their number or username and you have 'opt-in permission from the recipient confirming that they wish to receive subsequent messages or calls from you'; best practice is 'separate opt-in by specific message category' and to 'Clearly communicate the value of receiving this information.' (2) Opt-out: 'You must respect all requests (either on or off WhatsApp) by a person to block, discontinue, or otherwise opt out of communications from you'; 'Do not confuse, deceive, defraud, mislead, spam, or surprise people with your communications.' (3) Templates and the window: 'You may only initiate conversations using an approved Message Template', used 'only for its designated purpose'; free replies are allowed inside 'the 24-hour customer service window, which opens and resets with each user message'; outside it, templates only. Automated replies 'must also have available prompt, clear, and direct escalation paths' (human agent, phone, email, web, store or form). (4) Categories (Meta developer docs): 'Only authentication templates can be used to send a one-time passcode'; 'URLs, media, and emojis are not allowed' in authentication templates; utility templates are 'typically triggered by a user action or request' and 'non-promotional'; mixed utility and promo content is marketing, and Meta can change a misfiled template to MARKETING. (5) Content: 'Don't share or ask people to share full length individual payment card numbers, financial account numbers, personal ID card numbers, or other sensitive identifiers'; no impersonation of another business; no offensive or sexually explicit content; no discrimination; no promoting listed restricted goods (firearms, alcohol and tobacco, drugs, medical and healthcare products, currency and ICOs, real-money gambling, adult services, dating, multi-level marketing, payday loans and debt collection) except the country-limited Regulated Verticals; catalogs and selling follow the Meta Commerce Policy; the Platform may not be used by political parties, candidates or campaigns. (6) AI: providers of LLMs and general-purpose AI assistants are 'strictly prohibited from accessing or using the WhatsApp Business Platform' to offer them 'when such technologies are the primary (rather than incidental or ancillary) functionality' (Meta terms); TechCrunch reports this 'doesn't affect businesses that are using AI to serve customers'.
